literary_identity: The leading Caroline dramatist; a prolific author of comedies of fashionable London manners and of tragedies and tragicomedies, whose work T. S. Eliot called the 'last of the Elizabethan playwrights' and whose verse lyric 'Death the Leveller' remains famous.
biography: Born September 1596 in London, educated at Merchant Taylors' School, St John's College, Oxford, and St Catharine's, Cambridge. Converted to Catholicism, he taught school then turned to the stage, writing some thirty plays for the King's Men and Queen Henrietta's Men (1625–42), including The Wedding, Hyde Park, The Cardinal, and The Lady of Pleasure. During the Civil Wars he served as secretary to the royalist Earl of Newcastle; at the Restoration his old plays were revived with success. He died on 29 October 1666 in London, reportedly perishing with his wife in the Great Fire's aftermath.
literary_profile: The chronicler of Caroline fashionable society, whose comedies of intrigue, gallantry, and manners look forward to Restoration comedy, and whose tragedies show the late Jacobean taste for moral complexity and rhetorical set pieces.
stylistic_characteristics: Polished verse and prose; witty, fashionable dialogue; intricate plots of courtship and intrigue; sententious moralising; and a lyric grace ('Only the actions of the just / Smell sweet and blossom in the dust').
intellectual_concerns: Manners, fashion, and the morals of the town; love, honour, and gallantry; political corruption and tyranny; death and the levelling of rank; and the fate of virtue.
historical_significance: Shirley was the principal dramatist of the Caroline theatre and the direct model for Restoration comedy; his plays kept the professional drama alive in style until the theatres closed in 1642.
biographical_uncertainty: Shirley's life is documented in outline; the exact dates and authorship of some plays, and of his posthumous Six New Plays (1653), remain matters of scholarship.

literary_identity: Caroline tragedian; the most intense and morbidly introspective of the later Jacobean-Caroline dramatists, author of 'Tis Pity She's a Whore, The Broken Heart, and Love's Sacrifice, whose plays explore transgressive passion, melancholy, and divided conscience.
biography: Born c. 1586 at Ilsington, Devon (baptised 17 April), educated at Exeter College, Oxford and the Middle Temple (called to the bar 1620). He collaborated with Dekker, Rowley, and Webster on comedies and tragicomedies in the 1620s before writing his surviving solo tragedies in the early 1630s: Love's Sacrifice (1633), 'Tis Pity She's a Whore (1633), The Broken Heart (1633), and Perkin Warbeck (1634), with later comedies The Fancies Chaste and Noble (1638) and The Lady's Trial (1639). Little of his later life is recorded; he died c. 1639–40.
literary_profile: The tragedian of forbidden and self-destructive passion, whose plays probe incest, jealousy, and Stoic endurance with a melancholic, casuistical intensity and a detached moral ambiguity.
stylistic_characteristics: Grave, formal blank verse; rhetorical lamentation and masque-like set pieces; a preoccupation with melancholy and Stoic self-mastery; and a disturbing moral neutrality toward transgression.
intellectual_concerns: Incestuous and forbidden desire; honour, jealousy, and reputation; melancholy and the divided self; Stoic endurance of suffering; and the ethics of passion versus social law.
historical_significance: Ford is the last great tragedian before the closing of the theatres; 'Tis Pity She's a Whore and The Broken Heart are central to the Caroline tragic canon and to modern interest in the psychology and transgression of Renaissance drama.
biographical_uncertainty: Very little of Ford's biography is known; his birth and death dates are approximate, many of his works are lost, and his collaborations complicate attribution.

literary_identity: Caroline comic dramatist and former servant and protégé of Ben Jonson; author of robust, satirical city comedies such as The Antipodes, A Jovial Crew, and The Sparagus Garden, prized for their low-life energy and social observation.
biography: Born c. 1590 (records are sparse); he served Ben Jonson as a menial and became his literary protégé ('my man', Jonson called him). From 1629 he wrote some fifteen comedies for the Salisbury Court, Queen Henrietta's, and other companies, including The Northern Lass (1629), Bartholomew Fair-ish city comedies, The Antipodes (1638), and A Jovial Crew (1641), the last major play before the theatres closed. He signed a notorious contract with the Salisbury Court theatre (1635–40). He survived into the Interregnum, dependent and impoverished, dying in 1652.
literary_profile: The most Jonsonian of the Caroline comic writers, whose satirical, energetic comedies of London low life, country gentry, and humours anticipate the social breadth of Restoration comedy.
stylistic_characteristics: Vigorous prose and verse comedy; satire of humours and social types; realistic London and rustic settings; bawdy energy; and intricate farcical plotting.
intellectual_concerns: Social satire and the manners of town and country; wit, folly, and pretension; the world of beggars, players, and gallants; and the comic correction of humours.
historical_significance: Brome is the most important comic dramatist of the 1630s after Jonson's decline; his plays offer an unparalleled social portrait of Caroline London and directly influenced Restoration comedy, and A Jovial Crew was long popular in adaptation.
biographical_uncertainty: Brome's life is very poorly documented; his birth date is conjectural, and the dating and company attribution of several plays are uncertain.

literary_identity: Poet, playwright, and impresario; the crucial bridge between the Caroline and Restoration stages, who kept drama alive during the Interregnum with 'entertainments' and the proto-opera The Siege of Rhodes, held one of the two Restoration theatre patents, and introduced women players and scenery to the English stage.
biography: Born February 1606 in Oxford, son of a vintner (legend, fostered by Davenant, claimed Shakespeare as his father and godfather). He wrote masques and plays for the Caroline court, succeeded Jonson as poet laureate (1638), and was knighted (1651) for royalist service. During the Commonwealth he produced The Siege of Rhodes (1656) at Rutland House — often called the first English opera — evading the ban on plays as 'moral representations'. Imprisoned and pardoned for his part in royalist plots, he survived to hold, with Thomas Killigrew, the royal patent of 1660 that reopened the theatres; his Duke's Company introduced moveable scenery and, in 1660, the first professional actresses. He adapted Shakespeare (with Dryden, The Tempest, 1667) and died on 7 April 1668, buried in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: The impresario-poet who modernised the English stage, blending masque, opera, and neoclassical drama, and whose Gondibert (1651) experimented with a new quatrain epic form praised by Hobbes.
stylistic_characteristics: Masque and spectacle; the experimental four-line stanza of Gondibert; neoclassical dramatic theory; heroic and operatic forms; and a verse of public, philosophical ambition.
intellectual_concerns: The reform and moral justification of drama; Platonic and heroic virtue (Gondibert); the integration of music, scenery, and spectacle; royalist loyalty; and the new stagecraft.
historical_significance: Davenant founded the institutional and technical shape of the Restoration theatre — its patents, scenery, women players, and operatic ambitions — and mentored the young Dryden; without him the continuity of English drama across the Interregnum would have been broken.
biographical_uncertainty: The claim that Davenant was Shakespeare's biological son is legend, not fact; his biography is otherwise well documented through theatre records and state papers.

literary_identity: Restoration dramatist; author of the two fiercest comedies of manners, The Country Wife (1675) and The Plain Dealer (1676), whose savage wit and moral seriousness about lust, hypocrisy, and jealousy set him apart from his more elegant contemporaries.
biography: Born c. 1640–41 at Clive, Shropshire, educated at Queen's College, Oxford, the Middle Temple, and in France (where he briefly became a Catholic before reverting). He served at sea in the Second Dutch War and moved in court circles. His plays — Love in a Wood (1671), The Gentleman Dancing-Master (1672), The Country Wife (1675), and The Plain Dealer (1676) — won him fame but little money. A secret marriage to the Countess of Drogheda ruined him; he spent seven years in the Fleet for debt, was briefly reconciled to his father, and lived in obscurity and poverty until, in old age, he married a young heiress days before his death on 1 January 1716, leaving his manuscripts to the young Alexander Pope.
literary_profile: The most savage and morally earnest of the Restoration comic writers, whose comedies expose sexual appetite, jealousy, and hypocrisy with a harsh, near-Jacobean intensity beneath the manners-comedy surface.
stylistic_characteristics: Biting, energetic dialogue; intrigue plotting drawn from Molière and the Spanish; sexual frankness and dark comedy; and a moral seriousness unusual in the comedy of manners.
intellectual_concerns: Lust, jealousy, and cuckoldry; social and sexual hypocrisy; the corruption of town and country; misanthropy and plain dealing; and the vanity of pretence.
historical_significance: The Country Wife and The Plain Dealer are among the greatest English comedies; Wycherley's moral ferocity influenced Congreve and later satirists, and his late-life friendship with Pope linked Restoration and Augustan letters.
major_influences: Lope de Vega and the Spanish comedia
biographical_uncertainty: Wycherley's birth year is uncertain (c. 1640–41) and much of his biography, especially his marriages and debts, is recorded only in anecdotal sources.

literary_identity: The greatest master of the comedy of manners; author of The Way of the World (1700), Love for Love (1695), and the tragedy The Mourning Bride (1697), whose flawless comic prose and brilliant repartee represent the summit of English wit comedy.
biography: Born 24 January 1670 at Bardsey, Yorkshire, son of an army officer; raised in Ireland and educated at Kilkenny and Trinity College, Dublin. He came to London, studied law at the Middle Temple, and astonished the town with The Old Bachelor (1693), followed by The Double Dealer (1693), Love for Love (1695), and The Mourning Bride (1697, the most successful tragedy of the decade). His masterwork The Way of the World (1700) was coolly received, and, sensitive to criticism and enjoying a comfortable government sinecure and the friendship of the Whig Junto (and a long liaison with Henrietta Godolphin, Duchess of Marlborough), he wrote little after 1700. He died on 19 January 1729 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: The consummate artist of comic prose, whose plays achieve a perfection of wit, structure, and tone — 'the prose Shakespeare' — treating the negotiation of love, marriage, and money in a society of manners with ironic elegance.
stylistic_characteristics: Brilliantly epigrammatic prose; the 'proviso' scene of negotiated marriage; balanced, ironic repartee; elegant plotting; and, in The Mourning Bride, sonorous blank-verse declamation.
intellectual_concerns: Wit and true wit; love, marriage, and money; hypocrisy, affectation, and scandal; the social code of the town; and the relation of art and manners.
historical_significance: The Way of the World is universally regarded as the finest comedy of manners in English; Congreve defined the genre, influenced Sheridan and Wilde, and his tragic lines ('Musick has charms to soothe a savage breast') became proverbial.
biographical_uncertainty: Congreve's life is well documented; his early retirement from writing is explained by his finances, health, and sensitivity to criticism, though the reasons remain partly conjectural.

literary_identity: Restoration wit and dramatist; the originator of the comedy of manners with The Comical Revenge (1664), She Would if She Could (1668), and especially The Man of Mode (1676), which created the ideal rake-hero Dorimant and set the pattern for Wycherley and Congreve.
biography: Born c. 1635–36, probably in Berkshire; educated at Trinity Hall, Cambridge and the Middle Temple, with time in France. His first play, The Comical Revenge (1664), mixed verse and prose; She Would if She Could (1668) was less successful; but The Man of Mode (1676), with its rake Dorimant (thought to caricature Rochester) and the witty Harriet, was the triumph of the age. Etherege led a dissolute court life, was knighted (1679), and served as diplomat at Regensburg (1685–89), where he famously neglected business for pleasure. He returned after the Revolution and died c. 1691–92, possibly in Paris.
literary_profile: The elegant, careless founder of the comedy of manners, whose plays established the prose of witty gallantry, the rake-hero, and the social world of the town that the genre would perfect.
stylistic_characteristics: Sparkling prose repartee; the rake and the witty heroine; intrigue and sexual politics; a light, ironic tone; and a deliberate 'careless' elegance.
intellectual_concerns: Wit, gallantry, and libertinism; courtship and marriage as social negotiation; fashion, affectation, and the town; and the amoral play of desire.
historical_significance: The Man of Mode is the first great comedy of manners and defined its conventions; Etherege's rake-hero and social comedy directly shaped Wycherley, Congreve, and the whole tradition of English wit comedy.
biographical_uncertainty: Etherege's birth and death dates are approximate, his diplomatic correspondence survives but his private life is thinly documented, and he has been confused with a namesake.

literary_identity: Dramatist, Whig, and poet laureate; a self-professed disciple of Jonson who wrote vigorous comedies of humours and low life (Epsom Wells, The Squire of Alsatia) and whose quarrel with Dryden made him the target of Mac Flecknoe and the 'Og' of Absalom and Achitophel.
biography: Born c. 1642 at Stanthall, Norfolk, educated at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn. A committed Protestant and Whig, he wrote some eighteen plays, including the comedies The Sullen Lovers (1668), Epsom Wells (1672), and The Squire of Alsatia (1688), the tragedy Psyche (1674), and the anti-Catholic The Lancashire Witches (1681). He succeeded Dryden as poet laureate and historiographer royal after the Revolution of 1688 (Dryden, a Catholic, having been deprived). He died on 19 November 1692.
literary_profile: The Jonsonian satirist-comedian of the Restoration, whose plays championed 'humours' comedy, Protestant Whiggism, and a plain, moral, low-comic realism against what he saw as the immorality and wit of Dryden's party.
stylistic_characteristics: Comedy of humours and dialect; realistic low-life and provincial settings; moral satire; verse prologues and epilogues of political bite; and, in his operas and masques, spectacle.
intellectual_concerns: Protestant and Whig politics; the satire of vice, foppery, and popery; the moral purpose of comedy; Jonsonian 'humours'; and the defence of plain English sense.
historical_significance: Shadwell's importance lies both in his substantial, socially observant comedies and in his role as Dryden's antagonist — his defeat in the Mac Flecknoe quarrel made him a permanent emblem of literary dullness, though modern critics have reassessed his real comic talent.
biographical_uncertainty: Shadwell's birth year is approximate; the Dryden–Shadwell quarrel is well documented, though Shadwell's reputation suffered from its partisan literary afterlife.

literary_identity: Restoration tragedian; the master of pathetic, sentimental tragedy in blank verse, whose The Orphan (1680) and above all Venice Preserv'd (1682) were the most performed serious plays of the eighteenth century until superseded by later taste.
biography: Born 3 March 1652 at Trotton, Sussex, educated at Winchester and Christ Church, Oxford, then briefly a soldier in Flanders. Turning to the stage, he wrote comedies (Alcibiades, 1675; Friendship in Fashion, 1678), the tragicomedies Titus and Berenice and Cheats of Scapin (1676–77), and his great tragedies The Orphan (1680) and Venice Preserv'd (1682), the latter inspired by the Popish Plot and starring the actors Thomas Betterton and Elizabeth Barry, with whom he was infatuated. He also wrote the verse tragedy Caius Marius (1679). He died in poverty on 14 April 1685, supposedly choking on bread after a long fast.
literary_profile: The poet of 'pathetic' tragedy, whose heroines and heroes of overwhelming, tender passion moved audiences to tears and created the sentimental mode that dominated the serious stage for a century.
stylistic_characteristics: Passionate, tender blank verse; the tragedy of suffering innocence; scenes of heightened pathetic emotion; and a rhetoric designed to elicit tears and pity.
intellectual_concerns: Love, friendship, and betrayal; suffering innocence and female distress; political conspiracy and loyalty; the passions and their tragic cost; and sentimental virtue.
historical_significance: Venice Preserv'd held the stage continuously until the 1830s and was admired by Dryden, Pope, and Johnson; Otway's pathetic tragedy shaped the sentimental drama of the eighteenth century and the acting careers of Betterton and Barry.
biographical_uncertainty: Otway's life is documented but romanticised; the story of his death by choking is traditional, and details of his military and amorous life are partly anecdotal.

literary_identity: The first English woman to earn a living as a professional writer; a prolific playwright, poet, novelist, and (she claimed) secret agent, whose The Rover (1677) and the novella Oroonoko (1688) are landmarks of Restoration drama and of the early English novel.
biography: Born c. 1640, probably at Canterbury; she claimed (in Oroonoko) to have lived as a girl in Surinam, though this is disputed. She may have served as a royalist intelligence agent in Antwerp (as 'Astrea') during the Second Dutch War, was imprisoned for debt in 1668, and from the 1670s supported herself by writing for the stage. She produced some nineteen plays — comedies including The Rover (1677, 1681), The Feign'd Curtizans (1679), and The Lucky Chance (1686), and the tragicomedies Oroonoko (adapted) and The Widow Ranter (1689) — as well as poetry, translations (from Fontenelle and La Rochefoucauld), and the prose fiction Oroonoko; or, The Royal Slave (1688), Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister, and The Fair Jilt. A staunch royalist and Tory, she wrote for James II's cause and died on 16 April 1689, buried in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: The professional woman of letters who wrote with energy and commercial acumen across every genre, defending a woman's right to write and to pleasure while exposing the sexual and colonial politics of her age.
stylistic_characteristics: Vigorous comic prose and verse; the rake and the resourceful heroine; bawdy wit and sexual frankness; narrative prose blending travel, romance, and reportage; and political and amorous verse.
intellectual_concerns: Women's authorship, sexuality, and economic independence; libertinism and the double standard; slavery, colonialism, and the 'noble slave'; royalist and Tory politics; and the professional writer's life.
historical_significance: Behn is the first Englishwoman to have lived by her pen and a founding figure of the English novel; Oroonoko is an early anti-slavery narrative, and her recovery by Virginia Woolf and feminist criticism has made her central to women's literary history.
biographical_uncertainty: Behn's early life, her Surinam voyage, her marriage, and her espionage are all disputed or thinly documented; she freely fictionalised her own biography, making the factual record uncertain.

literary_identity: Irish-born Restoration dramatist; author of the pathetic tragedy The Fatal Marriage (1694) and of the stage adaptation of Behn's Oroonoko (1695), which held the repertory for over a century and made the 'noble slave' a staple of the eighteenth-century theatre.
biography: Born 1660 at Stranorlar, County Donegal, educated at Trinity College, Dublin and the Middle Temple. He came to London, was befriended by Dryden (for whom he wrote a prologue), and produced comedies (The Wives' Excuse, 1691; The Maid's Last Prayer, 1693) and tragedies. His Oroonoko (1695), adapting Behn's novella into a tragedy with a comic subplot, and The Fatal Marriage (1694), built for the actress Elizabeth Barry, were enormously successful. He made a fortune from an Irish sinecure and a government post, retired from the stage early, and lived to the great age of 86, dying on 28 May 1746.
literary_profile: The successful practitioner of pathetic tragedy and the adapter who transmitted Behn's Oroonoko to the eighteenth-century stage in a form that shaped the period's imagination of slavery and noble suffering.
stylistic_characteristics: Pathetic, sentimental blank verse; tragic suffering heroines; a mixture of tragedy and comic intrigue (in Oroonoko); and a commercially astute dramaturgy.
intellectual_concerns: Suffering innocence and pathetic tragedy; slavery and the 'noble savage'; love, marriage, and misfortune; and the moral appeal to pity.
historical_significance: Southerne's Oroonoko was the standard stage version of the story for 150 years and the vehicle through which Behn's anti-slavery narrative reached mass audiences; his pathetic tragedies exemplify the sentimental turn of Restoration serious drama.
biographical_uncertainty: Southerne's life is documented; the extent of Dryden's hand in his early work and the sources of some plays are matters of scholarship.

literary_identity: Restoration playwright and, later, the great baroque architect of Blenheim Palace and Castle Howard; his bawdy, energetic comedies The Relapse (1696) and The Provoked Wife (1697) revived the Restoration comedy of manners at the turn of the century.
biography: Born January 1664 (baptised 24 January) in London, of a Flemish merchant family; educated at Chester and briefly a soldier and an officer in the East India Company. Imprisoned in the Bastille (1690–92) on suspicion of espionage, he turned to the stage on his release, producing The Relapse; or, Virtue in Danger (1696) and The Provoked Wife (1697), huge successes that scandalised the reformers. He also wrote The False Friend (1702) and farces. From about 1702 he became, astonishingly, a leading architect (Knighted 1714), designing Blenheim Palace and Castle Howard in the English baroque. He died on 26 March 1726.
literary_profile: The robust, good-humoured comic writer whose plays are broad, bawdy, and structurally bold, contrasting with Congreve's polish; his Lord Foppington and his treatment of marital misery are Restoration comedy at its most energetic.
stylistic_characteristics: Broad farce and bawdy wit; energetic, colloquial prose; bold double plots; memorable comic types (Lord Foppington); and a genial, unsentimental view of vice.
intellectual_concerns: Sexual appetite and marriage; social pretension and foppery; virtue and its dangers; and the comedy of manners under moral attack.
historical_significance: Vanbrugh's comedies are the last great works of Restoration comic drama and a bridge to eighteenth-century comedy; his subsequent career as England's foremost baroque architect makes him a unique figure in the arts.
biographical_uncertainty: Vanbrugh's early life (soldiering, Bastille) is documented but partly legendary; his birth date is approximate, and the transition to architecture is remarkable but well recorded.

literary_identity: Anglo-Irish Restoration-early Augustan dramatist; author of the lively, humane comedies The Constant Couple (1699), The Inconstant (1702), and his masterpiece The Beaux' Stratagem (1707), which infused the comedy of manners with warmth, Irish vigour, and social observation.
biography: Born c. 1677–78 at Londonderry, educated at Trinity College, Dublin. He became an actor (stabbing a fellow-player in a stage duel), then a playwright with Love and a Bottle (1698) and The Constant Couple (1699), whose Sir Harry Wildair was hugely popular. He served briefly as an army officer and recruiting agent (the material for The Recruiting Officer, 1706). Despite success he died poor and young on 29 April 1707, weeks after The Beaux' Stratagem. His plays' gaiety and humanity mark the transition from Restoration wit to the gentler comedy of the eighteenth century.
literary_profile: The comic dramatist who softened Restoration intrigue with warmth, humour, and social realism, creating breezy, well-constructed comedies of love, roguery, and provincial life.
stylistic_characteristics: Lively, humorous prose; brisk plotting; roguish, charming heroes; Irish and provincial colour; and a humane, genial comic tone.
intellectual_concerns: Love, courtship, and roguery; money and marriage; the world of the provinces and the recruiting office; and the good humour of human frailty.
historical_significance: The Beaux' Stratagem and The Recruiting Officer are among the most enduring comedies of the period, continuously performed and admired for their vitality; Farquhar bridged Restoration and Augustan comedy and influenced Goldsmith and Sheridan.
biographical_uncertainty: Farquhar's birth year is uncertain (1677 or 1678) and details of his life are thin; the anecdotes of his stage-duel and poverty are traditional.

literary_identity: Actor-manager, playwright, poet laureate, and autobiographer; his comedy Love's Last Shift (1696) inaugurated 'sentimental comedy', and his flamboyant An Apology for the Life of Colley Cibber (1740) is a vivid memoir of the Restoration stage — though Pope made him the hero of The Dunciad.
biography: Born 6 November 1671 in London, son of the sculptor Caius Gabriel Cibber; educated at the Free School, Grantham. He joined the stage as an actor and wrote some twenty-five plays, beginning with Love's Last Shift (1696), whose reformed rake launched sentimental comedy; his adaptations of Shakespeare and Molière and farces like The Non-Juror were commercially astute. He became a leading actor-manager (patentee of Drury Lane, 1710), poet laureate (1730, a deeply unpopular appointment), and wrote his celebrated Apology (1740). He died on 12 December 1757.
literary_profile: The shrewd, vain, and gifted man of the theatre whose sentimental comedies and lively memoir shaped eighteenth-century drama and whose laureateship made him the byword for poetic dullness.
stylistic_characteristics: Sentimental, moralising comedy; theatrical savvy and adaptation; a lively, self-promoting prose in the Apology; and occasional verse of modest quality.
intellectual_concerns: Moral reform and sentimental virtue; the business and life of the theatre; vanity and self-justification; and the reform of comedy toward feeling.
historical_significance: Cibber founded sentimental comedy and left in his Apology one of the most valuable first-hand accounts of the Restoration and early Georgian stage; his laureateship and feud with Pope secured his immortality as the 'king of dunces'.
biographical_uncertainty: Cibber's Apology is candid but self-serving; details are embellished for effect, and his reputation was distorted by Pope's satire.

literary_identity: Restoration tragedian; the leading exponent of heroic drama after Dryden, whose bombastic but powerful The Rival Queens (1677) held the stage for two centuries, and who collaborated with Dryden on Oedipus and The Duke of Guise.
biography: Born c. 1653 at Waltham Abbey, Essex, son of a clergyman; educated at Westminster and Trinity College, Cambridge. He turned from brief attempts at law and teaching to the stage, writing heroic plays and tragedies including The Tragedy of Nero (1674), Sophonisba (1675), Gloriana (1676), and his great success The Rival Queens; or, The Death of Alexander the Great (1677). He collaborated with Dryden on Oedipus (1679) and The Duke of Guise (1682). Suffering from mental illness and alcoholism, he was confined in Bedlam (1684–88); released after the Revolution, he wrote The Princess of Cleve (1689) and died in poverty on 6 May 1692.
literary_profile: The passionate, sometimes ranting tragedian of the Restoration, whose heroic and blank-verse tragedies of overwhelming emotion and elevated rhetoric were enormously popular and long-lived on the stage.
stylistic_characteristics: Elevated, bombastic rhetoric; heroic couplets and blank verse; scenes of violent passion and grandiose declamation; and, at best, real pathos and poetic power.
intellectual_concerns: Heroic passion, love, and glory; political conspiracy and tyranny; madness and the extremes of emotion; and the fate of great figures.
historical_significance: The Rival Queens was one of the most frequently performed plays from the Restoration into the nineteenth century; Lee's heroic tragedy carried the mode to its popular peak and influenced the acting style of the age.
biographical_uncertainty: Lee's birth year is approximate and his biography, including his madness and Bedlam confinement, is documented but partly anecdotal.
